title: Vintage Card Grading (2026)
verdict: Vintage card grading at AGS uses tolerances set for older card stock and a flat $18 fee, so a valuable vintage card costs no more to grade than a common.

PSA and SGC are the names vintage buyers pay the most for, and on a high-end card that premium is worth their fees. Beckett has graded vintage for decades and adds subgrades. TAG is out: its site says it does not currently accept pre-1989 cards.

sections.h: What you get for the fee
list: A grade from 1 to 10 with decimal precision.
Eight subgrades: centering, corners, edges and surface, front and back.
A 3D heightmap of the surface, color-coded from green to red.
High-resolution images and centering data for both sides.
A sealed PMMA slab with the cert number on the label.
A permanent online record, reachable by cert number or shared link.
Check for trimming. Measure the card against a known genuine copy.
Look for recoloring on edges and corners under magnification.
Expect off-center cuts. Many vintage sets were cut loosely, and graders allow for it differently.
Confirm the grader takes the card. TAG does not accept pre-1989 cards.
Check how the fee is set. Declared-value pricing costs more on valuable vintage.

ranking.fit: Owners of valuable vintage who do not want the grading fee to climb with the card.
ranking.lacks: Vintage buyers still pay the biggest premiums for PSA and SGC holders.
ranking.note: Vintage is graded with slightly different tolerances than modern cards. Miscuts and print errors are measured and graded.

ranking.fit: Pre-war and vintage sports, where SGC's holder is second only to PSA's.
ranking.lacks: Fees scale with declared value, and the base is a reported $50.

ranking.fit: High-end vintage, where a PSA holder brings the biggest premium.
ranking.lacks: Fees climb with declared value, which is exactly where vintage sits.

ranking.fit: Vintage collectors who want subgrades and no fee tied to card value.
ranking.lacks: A smaller vintage premium than PSA or SGC.

ranking.fit: Vintage on a budget, if the card is worth less than the tier cap.
ranking.lacks: Tier caps bite on valuable vintage.

why: Vintage cards are accepted and graded against tolerances set for older stock. Because the fee is flat, a five-figure card costs the same to grade as a common. At PSA and SGC the fee climbs with declared value, and CGC's tiers are capped by it.

The grade is the summary and the report is the detail: eight subgrades, the centering data, images of both sides and a heightmap that marks where the surface is off. It is yours to download, and a buyer can reach it from the cert number.

Authentication is part of the scan. AGS says its system flags trimmed cards, recolored edges, altered surfaces and outright fakes, and it stores a digital fingerprint of every card. Anyone can check a slab by entering the cert number on agscard.com.

faq.a: On the same four points as modern cards, with allowances for how older cards were printed and cut. AGS grades vintage with slightly different tolerances and measures miscuts and print errors.

faq.q: Do graders charge more for valuable cards?
faq.a: Several do. PSA and SGC price by declared value, and CGC caps each tier by card value and moves a card up if it is worth more. AGS, Beckett, TAG and ISA say they add no upcharge for value.

Signed cards are accepted for grading. If you need the autograph itself authenticated, use a grader that sells that service. Beckett lists a $5 autograph add-on, and CGC offers autograph authentication.

faq.q: Do AGS slabs hold resale value?
faq.a: AGS slabs sell, and the report gives buyers something to check. PSA holders still bring the highest prices on most cards. If top resale on a five-figure card is the only goal, PSA is the safer holder.

faq.q: Who owns PSA, SGC and Beckett?
faq.a: Collectors. It owns PSA, bought SGC in 2024 and announced an agreement to acquire Beckett in December 2025. Each keeps its own brand.
